speechtext: ANNOUNCEMENT OP MOVEMENT OF FIRST GROUP FROM CANADA TO JAPAN	.

Mr. Speaker, because of the general interest in the matter I thought I should inform hon. members that definite arrangements have now been made for the movement of the first group of Japanese nationals from Canada to Japan. The group being sent consists of those who elected to be repatriated to Japan and who have .not asked
[Mr. Coldwell.l
that their requests be cancelled; in other words the group being dealt with at present are those who have asked for the privilege of returning to Japan, and who are being assisted to go.- The details of the arrangement I think are well known to hon. members.
In the class I have been speaking of will be those who are perfectly satisfied to be repatriated to Japan, and it is anticipated there will be approximately 1,500, including men, women and children. Most of them are coming from the settlements in the interior of British Columbia, but a few are coming from Alberta and Manitoba and some who have been in internment camps at Angler, Ontario. All arrangements have been made for the movement to Vancouver, and it is anticipated the first boat will leave Vancouver on May 28, carrying some 680, while the second boat will be leaving about the end of May carrying approximately 900.
While on the subject I might say that we will defer deportation proceedings pending the decision of the privy council, to which authority the case has been appealed. The department is proceeding as rapidly as possible with the dispersal of others to various parts of Canada, seeing to it that only a limited number are sent to each place and emphasizing placement in agriculture or lumbering or logging.

May I say that I wish the Prime Minister a pleasant voyage and a safe return from his proposed journey. I wish him good luck for Canada in the work he proposes to do. There are three questions to which I should like a reply before he goes. I have sent him copies of these questions and I am sorry I was not able to send them earlier.

The second question is with regard to the statement made by President Truman over the radio a week ago in connection with a joint defence plan for the future of America. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTURE FOR LONDON ON MAY 13 TO ATTEND PRIME MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
May I express to the leaders of the different parties and those who are supporting them, as well as to hon. members on this side of the house, my very warm appreciation of the kind manner in which they have recognized the necessity of my going overseas for a short time and for the good wishes they have extended for that sojourn abroad.
The leader of the opposition has relieved my mind of one consideration when he assures me
The Prime Minister

that he will see that the government carries on successfully while I am away. To that extent, I shall be tremendously relieved. My hon. friend the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has said that he hoped I would be more communicative. May I say to him that I have found that more public men get into trouble from what they say than from what they do not say. If I am not over-communicative at times it is because from long experience in public affairs I have learned that silence is often golden where speech is merely silvern.
May I say to hon. members that I have been very much of two opinions as to what my duty was at the moment in the matter of going overseas. Early in the year I received from the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom a communication saying that he hoped a meeting of all the prime ministers might be held in London, I understood in connection with the approaching peace conference at Paris. It seemed to me that a meeting of prime ministers held at that time would probably bring together the prime ministers from the different parts of the empire, and as I had planned to attend the peace conference in Paris, that seemed to be a suitable time for such a meeting. I therefore said that I would welcome such an arrangement. However, on communications being sent to the different nations of the commonwealth, it was found that Mr. Chifley, Prime Minister of Australia, could be in England only at a certain time; that Mr. Fraser, Prime Minister of New Zealand, would not find it possible to make the trip himself, and that General Smuts of South Africa could not leave South Africa before a certain time. Early in February I had been a party to the agreement with the provinces that the dominion-provincial conference would meet here at Ottawa at the time it did, so I was obliged to say that I could not possibly think of going over until that conference was concluded.
The result was that the idea of having the prime ministers meet collectively on a particular date was given up, and instead it was suggested that there might be consultations between the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and one or more of his ministers and the prime ministers of the dominions arranged in different stages. Hon. members have seen that such has been the procedure that has been followed, that certain consultations have already been held. To permit of my being present there has been a postponement of some of the consultations until next week or the week after.
I wish it were not necessary to go because I feel that my duty just at this time is 
primarily in Canada, When we have the important questions that have been referred to this afternoon concerning the discussion of relations between the provinces and ourselves, as well as other important matters coming up. I do not see how I or persons holding a similar office ' in the different dominions can be expected to be in Britain all at the same time. I think a man's first duty is to his own country and to his own parliament. If I had consulted my own feelings at this time I would have remained here, but I realize that there are reasons why consultation in reference to some of the matters that have been mentioned is advisable and I have given my word that I would go across to take part in those consultations. I plan to leave on Monday of next week.
I think it is important to realize that we have in this country and in all parts of the commonwealth a system of consultation which can be effected by means of cable, as was followed out throughout the years of the war, and which I believe is about as perfect as any system could be. It enables a prime minister when sitting in conference to speak with the authority of all his colleagues. I wish to make it perfectly clear that I am not going to attempt at any consultation to say what this government's opinion is with regard to questions of defence, questions of trade, preference and the like, because I am not one of those who pretend to speak for the entire cabinet without the opportunity of conferring with its members. I shall be very happy at any conference to give my views in a general way as to opinions that I think this country would wish to have fully considered. But as for presenting at a conference the official view of Canada in great matters of defence, trade and numerous other important questions, without the presence of the ministers who are responsible immediately concerned for the different departments of government and without the presence of their experts as well, I can assure the house that I shall be careful to refrain from committing anyone in a manner that is likely to occasion embarrassment.

1. Departmental administration, $163,190.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amount we are asking the house to vote this year for ordinary purposse is $13,692,713; that is an increase of $1,615,444 over the estimates of 1945-46.
In the four years preceding the war we had been following the policy of building up the agriculture estimates from a low in 1935 to the figure at which they had been five years previously ancT we had just about reached that level when war was declared. After war was declared we cut down the ordinary estimates for agriculture, but during the last two years we have again been building them up so that this year they are $1,615,444 higher than they were last year. The increases have been made up as follows: Scientific services, $913,591; experimental farms, $223,223; production services, $321,225; marketing services, $112,675, or
a total of $1,570,714; increase in administration, $44,730, making a total increase of $1,615,444.
The estimates of the department are divided into ordinary and special. Under special we are asking the committee to vote this year, $5,725,000, as against $5,126,700 a year ago. The increased amount of $598,300 is divided between P.F.R.A. and cheese. There is an increase of $1,122,000 in P.F.R.A., with an additional amount not yet determined which will be taken out of the $10,000,000 vote for reconstruction. The increased expenditure on cheese, for the purpose of promoting the production of better cheese, is $200,000, making $1,322,000. The difference between the increase in these two branches and the total increase is accounted for by reductions in prairie farm asistance. That figure has not been finally determined because it depends very much on the weather this year, and there is a possibility that the actual expenditure may go back to what it was a year ago.
The other has to do with wheat acreage reduction. The greater part of the difference is in wheat acreage reduction. During the last two years we have not been carrying on the policy of promoting wheat acreage reduction and for that reason no payments are being made and no vote is necessary for the purpose this year. So while the balance shows an increase of $598,300, there is an actual increase in the operative part of the estimates of $1,322,000.
I wanted to make those explanations before we start upon a consideration of the individual items, and would suggest, Mr. Chairman, subject of course to the opinion of the committee, that we can advance most satisfactorily and obtain the greatest amount of information by dealing with the matters which come under each item as we proceed. I assume that some hon. members will want to make general remarks before we do proceed on this basis, but I hope we can get to that basis as soon as possible.
Has there been any diminution of the amounts spent to encourage the manufacture of butter? The minister has stated that additional amounts have been spent to encourage the manufacture of cheese.

The amount spent in connection with cheese is not- to encourage increased production, but to encourage better quality. It is the premium we pay for the production of 94 and 93 score cheese, and, together with the assistance we give for putting in storage rooms and other equipment, to make it possible to produce a better product. The promotion of the production of each of these commodities will be dealt with under produc-
Supply-A gricul ture

tion, when we come to the votes in connection with production, and we shall be better able to determine at that time the amounts which are spent in various directions in order to promote production.
As a matter of fact, nothing has been voted to encourage the production of butter?

As far as I can recall at the moment, there is nothing specifically in the items, although we may come across something as we go through that might be so stated to be estimated; but that kind of expenditure is made out of the different items which provide for publicity, and we do take sums of money for promoting the production of different products from time to time during the year out of those amounts, and run advertisements in the papers and take other action to assist in obtaining higher production.

I hope the minister will not think that I am trying to ask him a lot of questions at once, but I have to go to the flag committee. Is the minister aware of the great number of dairy cattle that are being exported from eastern Quebec to the United States at the present time? I received a letter this morning which told me of thirty-two carloads of cattle passing through one station in the first two days of this week, and of a great number being taken across the international line by truck.' I am anxious to know whether the government deems that a policy which encourages the export of dairy cattle is a good policy, and whether anything is being done to stay the loss to Canada of those herds.

I repeat that I think we can more satisfactorily discuss that question when we get down to production. But I can give at the moment figures which will, I think, satisfy the hon. member that the problem is not as serious as might be suggested by figures taken from any locality. I will just take the last six years for which I have the records here. I have the records from 1928 down to the present, and could place them on Hansard if it were desired, showing, first, the exports of dairy cattle, and showing the numbers on farms; for every year but the present, the numbers on farms in June; and giving the number on farms in December of 1945.
Beginning at 1941, the number of exports was 13,719. I may say that that is the highest export that we have had since 1929. In 1942 the number was 19,139; in 1943, 37,327; 1944, 36,315; 1945, 47,304; 1946, down to March, 11.572.
The figures which one must put alongside of these are the figures of dairy cattle on farms in June of each year: 1941, 3,623,900; 1942, 3,680,500;	1943, 3,784,,700; 1944, 3,929,600;

1945, 3,998,200; and then in December of 1945, 4,012,600. In other words there has been a constant rise year by year down to the present of the number of dairy cattle on farms, until the figure of 3,929,600 in 1944 was the highest figure of any year from 1928 down to 1944, and, I assume, the highest figure right back through the years.
Would the minister explain why, if there is this increase in the number of dairy cattle-and I am not denying it-there has not been a corresponding increase in the production of milk?

There has. We will finish this question first. In 1945, as I indicated, the number wrent up to within two thousand of four million, which was much higher than any year we ever had; and in June 1945 we were over the four million mark.
The suggestion has been made that we might explain why there has been a lower production of milk, or, to put it in exact terms, I think the question was why there has not been a corresponding increase in the production of milk. Well, I am not in a position to state at the moment whether the increase is proportionate to the increase in the number of cows, although I am under the impression that the increase is greater than the increase in the number of cows. That is my opinion at the moment, unless I get something to the contrary which is not before me, that the production per cow has improved during that period; and it is natural that in times like these, when returns are good, farmers should get better stock and better bred stock on their farms. The actual fact is that last year the ' milk production was the highest on record. If it was not, the figures I have are not the same as those which my hon. friend has.

The point I would like to call to the attention of the minister is the precarious condition in which that branch of the dairy industry which lends itself to the making of butter finds itself to-day. The remarks of the minister referred to the dairy industry as a whole. He has explained on previous occasions what the department headed by himself has been able to do to capture a very desirable British market for cheese, and I think it is beyond dispute that milk converted into cheese yields a much greater return to the milk producer than does milk containing an equal quantity of butter-fat converted into butter. The figures the minister has given with regard to exports of cattle and the number of cattle on farms were general. They do not apply to Quebec and southeastern Quebec, to which my remarks on previous days in the house have been specially directed. In that area there is a vastly accelerated disposal of dairy herds to the United States. There is more than one reason for that. The first is that raw milk commands a much higher price in the United States than in Canada, and secondly there
appears to be great difficulty in getting labour to perform the work incidental to caring for herds on the farm and conveying the cream to the creamery.
The price of butter in Canada is much lower than in the United States. A quantity of milk converted into cheese gives the producer a much better return than if it were converted into butter. The dairy farmers find that it is not profitable for them to make butter and are therefore selling their herds. I believe the minister will find, if he compares the figures he has given of dairy cattle sold during the first four months of the current year, that the number per month is much greater than it was for the corresponding months last year, and the fear of many people who live in southeastern Quebec is that this most important of agricultural pursuits is going to be irreparably damaged if the price of butter be not raised so that the producers of butter can find enough profit in that pursuit to warrant retention of their herds rather than the sale of them across the line.
I agree with the minister that the dairy farmer in , southeastern Quebec has always derived a certain benefit from the . raising of dairy cattle of high productive capacity and the sale of them to the United States. In other days there was a very great trade in horses to the United States, and the trade in dairy cattle has been a source of revenue. But it has now reached the point where the sales are so greatly enhanced that the industry itself is jeopardized. Quebec, it is admitted, makes butter in preference to cheese. Canadian cheese commands a respected place in the foreign markets, the minister is to be commended on having secured these foreign markets for a commodity in the production of which we excel. But temperance in this, as in all matters, is a virtue; I ask the minister if he has considered the peril which overhangs the butter-producing industry in southeastern Quebec if he does not take the necessary steps to make one hundred pounds of milk of a given butterfat percentage when converted into butter give the farmer more nearly the return now obtained from one hundred pounds of milk converted into cheese. It seems to me that in order to get into the British market he has encouraged the manufacture of cheese to the detriment of the manufacture of butter, and that in consequence there is a shortage of butter which is accounted for by the disposal of herds and by the fact that the element of the community which manufactures the most blitter in Canada does not find it profitable to continue' in the manufacture of that, commodity.

Off cheese, because of the desire to get more butter. There was a shortage of butter. The subsidy was taken off cheese, with the result that cheese production went down. we were promoting the production of cheese at the moment as against the production of butter. We promoted the production' of cheese as against the production of butter at certain times during the war for certain reasons. The first was that Britain was pressing us for cheese. As hon. members of the committee know, Great .Britain stands at the top of the list of cheese eaters in the world, while Canada is at the bottom. The people of Great Britain eat the most cheese per head of population, while we eat the least, according to the records of the sixteen countries in which records are kept. We produce one of the kinds of cheese that the British like best, cheddar cheese. They have been willing to pay a premium for this even in ordinary times. That is the first reason the British wanted it. We tried to give them what they desired. Cheese has stored up in it a certain amount of butterfat in a way that permits it to be kept and therefore it is utilized in time of war.
The second reason is one that I believe most of those who are interested in agriculture are familiar with. There is an area in Canada which begins west of Toronto, perhaps as far west as Ingersoll, and extends down to Ottawa and as far as Kingston, then into Quebec as far as Three Rivers-we see an example of this area as we drive out from the city-where rock is very close to the surface and at times great boulders extend above the surface. But in between there are areas of luscious grass. We believe that if agriculture is to be continued successfully in this great area it is important that the farmers should be encouraged to produce cheese. We believe that if they are going to be encouraged to pro. duce cheese they must have a good market, and we think the only good market is in Great Britain. Therefore we have been trying to supply the best cheese, and I think we are putting out the highest graded cheese we have ever had in Canada, partly because of the premium we have paid for high grade cheese and largely because of the desire of the producers themselves to get the best possible product over in the greatest quantities. So we have been promoting the production of cheese. There is a question as to whether we have overdone it so far as providing sufficient butter for consumption in this country is concerned.
There is a third reason which I think should be mentioned here. We cannot produce butter in competition with New Zealand or Australia, and I do not think I need to go into the reasons. Those countries run their cows out the year around while we have to stable ours about seven months in the year if we are to
get much milk. When we attempt to place our butter on the British market in competition with their butter, we are not able to sell at the level they can sell at and still have a profit. What we have been trying to do is to maintain a Canadian market for butter and produce just about what is required by that market. As the opportunities to purchase have increased we have had greater difficulty in supplying the butter that is required in Canada. In spite of the fact that our creamery butter production was up on an average of about 40,000,000 pounds during the last three or four years as compared with the years preceding the war, we are still having difficulty in making the butter go round. For that reason, if for no other, there is some justification in believing that the time has come to promote the production of butter to a greater extent than it is being produced at the present time.
More people are eating it.
Yes. Some people who eat very little are eating what they require, while other people who eat more than they really require are having difficulty in getting what they want.
They cannot get it.

As my hon. friend says, they cannot get it. That is the position; that is what we are attempting to do* and those are the reasons why we are attempting to do it. For one thing, we want to keep the farmer in cheese production, and I am pleased to be able to say that in 1945 the production of cheese was higher than it has been for a long time, I think as far back as 1942.

Mr. Chairman, I have to leave the house in a few moments, and I should like to ask two questions before I go. One is on the matter we have now under discussion. I had not intended to deal with the subject, but since it has been referred to by other members I would like to ask a question.

Two and one-quarter billion dollars is a considerable amount of money, and when we spend only 819,000,000 on trying to boost that figure, it is not very much. When I had an opportunity of speaking in this house some time ago I made the statement that a country which could produce at the lowest cost, the highest quality article, would get the world market. The Minister of Agriculture this afternoon referred to that phase when he said that he did not consider it was possible for us to enter into successful competition with New Zealand, for instance, in the dairy industry, because we cannot compete- with their climatic conditions. I still believe as I have said before in the house, that in the last analysis we shall find all the nations of the world compelled to grow or produce or manufacture that thing which they can most economically grow or produce or manufacture.
Those countries will be able to capture the world market which can keep down costs of production. Costs of production establish the selling price of any commodity, and I was wondering how we can reduce production costs in agriculture.
There are two things that can be done if and when these production costs are reduced. The manufacturer or producer can secure more profits or, second, he can reduce the price at which he sells his commodity. I think the latter is the more desirable because in that way it will be possible to secure and make sure of a market, if we keep the price down and the quality up. But keeping the price down is a very important factor. With that thought in mind I give it as my opinion that tariffs, quotas and trade restrictions will have to go. I believe, as a matter of fact, they are out. Undoubtedly they have been war-producing. They have been the means of creating more ill will and trouble between nations than any other thing.
How can we cut down costs of production in agriculture? It is said that when Marquis wheat was king we lost one crop in five from a disease which we have all heard of and which is known as rust. That is, twenty per cent of our crop was lost because of this terrible scourge which we experienced for so many years in the western provinces. When eventually our plant breeders and plant path-63260- 87}
ologists were successful in producing a variety of wheat which was resistant to rust we saved one crop in five, or twenty per cent of our crop. In other words, our production costs were cut twenty per cent by the single factor of producing a variety of wheat resistant to rust. Any time that we conquer a plant disease, and any time that we conquer the effects of insect pests in agriculture, we are reducing our costs of production. This work is being done by our agricultural scientists, and I want to touch briefly on them in passing.
They have done and are still doing an extraordinarily good work in agriculture. It is of the highest importance that we should see to it that the services of these men are retained and encouraged in every way. I wish to acknowledge what the minister has done in this respect and to commend him for having started to raise the salaries of our agricultural scientists. I have in my hand a list of the men whose salaries have been raised, and I notice that the increases range all the way from $60 to $900 and that very few received only a $60 raise. Most of them received liberal raises. I have no doubt that this will be the means of encouraging these men to stay on the job and give us further assistance in our agricultural work.
Recently one of these men has been the means of discovering or originating another variety of wheat which has proved itself resistant to a pest known in the west as sawfly. Every year for a' good many years the losses from sawfly in the western provinces were anywhere from $15 to $20 million. So that it does seem as though we could afford to pay a reasonable salary to a man who can provide us with a variety of wheat which is resistant to the attacks of the sawfly. Losses in the western provinces from weeds amount to $70 million per annum. It would be worth a lot of money to us if some of these men could tell us how to avoid these weed losses. Another disease we have in the west is known as smut, and that costs us $20 million a year. If we could get rid of these things our production costs would be cut down and we would have a much better chance to compete in the world market. The agricultural scientist can save us all these losses if he is encouraged to do so, if the money is found for him to work with, in his laboratories and in other ways. These men must never be allowed to ease up on their work; it is never finished. I think I have told the house before, but it will bear repetition, that rust, which cost us so many million dollars a few years ago, and which we think we have conquered, could easily come at us again from another angle. We know there is a considerable number of varieties of rust. We have successfully stopped the

One aspect of agriculture about which I should like to talk for a few minutes and which I do not think has been discussed very much in this chamber, is the question of seed. In the last few years there has sprung up in this country, a seed industry the value of which is not appreciated by a great many people. We used to import a tremendous quantity of our seed. The situation is now changed, and we find ourselves with an export trade.in seed. It affects not only the prairie west but all the provinces. As a matter of fact some of the eastern provinces are gaining substantially from the growing of vegetable seed, as also is the far western province of British Columbia. Some of these figures might be interesting to the committee.
In 1939 this country produced 104,000 pounds of beans; in 1944 we produced 850,000 pounds of seed. Beet seed in this country increased from 4,000 pounds in 1939 to 80,000 pounds in 1944; cabbage seed, from 55 pounds to 6,500 pounds. ,Perhaps 6,500 pounds does not seem to be a very large quantity, but all things are relative, and a pound of cabbage seed is really a lot of seed. As a matter of fact-to come to one other kind of seed-in one ounce of tobacco seed there are roughly 90,000 seeds, which will plant ten acres. That is, one ounce of tobacco seed is in this respect the equivalent of fifteen bushels of wheat, for it will plant ten acres of land. The production of carrot seed has advanced from 10,000 to 221,000 pounds. There was no corn seed produced until 1943, and in that year we had 560,000 pounds, and so on all down the. line. There is a swede turnip seed which is grown by farmers in the maritimes, the amount having increased from 11,000 pounds in 1941 to 161,000 pounds in 1944; and that, as I have said before, is a tremendous lot of seed.	;
Tobacco seed is grown principally in Ontario, It is a very difficult thing to secure, because it has to be disease-free, and even the soil in which the tobacco plant is grown has to be sterilized before it can be safely used for this particular seed. Turnip seed is grown in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. The Laurentian seed, as it is called, provides hundreds upon hundreds 
of carloads of turnips grown from Canadian seed. In Nova Scotia, where this seed is being grown, the authorities marked off one area in which no other variety of seed was allowed to be grown except this one particular variety. It is the first time that any such experiment has been made. Beetroot seed is being grown in the maritimes to a great extent. I could name the number of thousands of pounds, but I do not wish to bore hon. members. But an interesting thing happened in this connection. One pound of a very special variety, Detroit dark red, was sent out to a trained grower, who returned the next year, for the one pound which he used, 275 pounds. The five other pounds which, constituted the remainder of that particular seed was sent out to untrained men. All this seed was lost; it became mixed with other varieties. Hydrid corn is another strongly entrenched seed product. It takes a long time to get a start. Twenty years are taken in developing the inbreds, and then the matching, as it is called, is done on an Ontario farm and produces a single cross which is used for the seed. There has been a tremendous increase in the amount of corn and a tremendous change in the type of plant which has been grown. It is stated that the type of plant grown from these hybrids has made possible the use of harvesting machinery for corn. Previously this was not possible because of the weakness of the stem; when there was a rain or a wind storm the plant went down; but now it stands up; machinery can be successfully used, and the saving has been tremendous. Vegetable seed is grown particularly in Ontario and British Columbia. There are six strains of onions developed by British Columbia groovers and now used all over the world. That is particularly interesting because I haye been told that the bulbs which are used to produce this onion seed are sometimes more valuable than the seed itself. Yet the growers continue to use them, and having established their market they have continued to keep it supplied.
In 1943-44 export seeds were as high as 4,500,000 pounds from Canada to the United Kingdom, consisting of carrots, beans, peas, cauliflower, lettuce, parsley, spinach and so on, and it is said that on the basis of average seeding and yields, these seeds produced 2,500,000 tons of food. In other words, that was the quantity of seeds that Canada shipped over in 1943-44 at a time when they were badly needed.
As regards cereals in the western provinces, in 1943 there were sown to wheat seventeen and a half million acres, representing 26,000,000 bushels of seed, and in the same year 15,000,000 acres were sown to oats, requiring 40,000,000

bushels of seed, and 8,500,000 acres of barley-requiring 13,000,000 bushels. In fact, in one year, 1940, we sowed 28,750,000 acres to wheat, which required 42,000,000 bushels of seed. That is a lot of seed, and that particular crop produced over $540,000,000 worth of wheat, even at fifty-two cents a bushel.
It can be seen, therefore, that this matter of seed is very important-important as a seed industry, and important as a means of securing good seed for our own country, and because seed plays such a fundamental part in our own production. I often wonder whether hon. members as they sweat over their garden patches pay sufficient attention to the quality of the seed they use, because all those backaches they endure at the end of a spade or shovel handle are wasted if they buy inferior seed. It is important that they should secure seed of the best quality.
There are in this country many agricultural organizations who are doing very good work but who are not known much outside their own orbit. They work in a little district or community and that is the only place in which they are known. There is such an organization, probably new to a great many members of this house, known as the Canadian Seed Growers' Association, or C.S.G.A. to use its initial letters. These people are responsible for taking care of all pure-line seeds.
A point that is not generally recognized is that when a plant breeder has secured what he was after, either a rust-resistant or an insect-resistant seed, he has only a very small quantity of seed, probably only a handful. The important thing is to get this handful out to the farmers in the country who require, in some years, 42,000,000 bushels of seed. But this very small handful is all there is, and. if it becomes mixed with anything else, it is useless because all its good qualities are lost. Someone has to take over the job of multiplying this small quantity of seed, and he has to take care in the process that it does not become fouled or mixed with anything else. This work requires training and patience and it takes a great deal of time. That is one of the principal objects of this organization known as the Canadian Seed Growers' Association. The association has not a very large membership, but these special seeds are handed over to the members for production and multiplication purposes, and they are the people who, because of special training and because of their willingness to devote their time to this kind of work, reproduce and multiply this small quantity into larger supplies, so that they may become available to the farmers of the land.
The scientific work is useless until all the farmers who require the seed can get it, and if these trained workers produce a rust-resistant seed all the farmers in the west should be supplied with it. It takes a great deal of time to multiply that seed, and purity is the important factor. Indeed, everything has to be taken into consideration. The land itself in which the seed is to be sown is generally a piece of summer-fallow. But that summer-fallow has to be cleared of all other growth and of all extraneous matter. If animals went across it last year it is absolutely useless for the purpose of growing the new variety of seed. If the machine that is used to do the seeding, the seed drill, is not thoroughly cleaned and every last seed taken out of it, it is of no use and it will spoil the whole set-up. It has to be thoroughly cleaned so that the crop will be absolutely pure. The same is true of every other implement used in the process. The threshing machine is probably the most difficult for the grower of pure-bred seed, because it is a physical impossibility to get every seed out of that piece of machinery. Any hon. members who have had experience with a thresher will realize the difficulties it presents. The result is that a good deal of pure seed will not be threshed in a threshing machine but by hand, with the use of a flail. Older members who were raised on farms will know what a flail is-a long stick with a short stick tied to it, the object being to swing it round the head without hitting the head but, instead, bringing it down on the sheaf of grain. In other words, we have to go back to the old methods because we are afraid of introducing foreign matter into the seed. Again, we have to use a floor that has not been used before because there may be in the cracks some grain from a previous occasion.
It is a terribly tedious job, and all these dangers of impurities getting into the seed are not the only things we have to worry about. There are other things the members of the association have to cope with.

Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: When the committee rose at six o'clock, I was trying to show the importance of an organization known as the Canadian Seed Growers' Association, and was pointing out the difficulties they encountered and the excellent work they were doing in keeping pure, certain lines of seed. The possibility and danger of mixtures which I
Supply-Agriculture

described was purely a mechanical matter. I mentioned those which might take place in the ground and those which might take place in the drills, and the machines used by these growers. When mixtures happened for these reasons, that would be purely a mechanical matter. However, other mixtures take place in the natural growth of the plants. You get cross-fertilization between plants of the same family, so that great care has to be exercised; and there is difficulty in differentiating between a cross-bred plant and one of pure strain. The members of the Canadian Seed Growers' Association have trained themselves so that without a great deal of difficulty they can recognize cross-breeding in the different plants, in their fields and plots. They have to keep great distances between those plants which are of pure strain, and those which are not. In the case of corn, for instance, there has to be at least a mile between the pure lines and other lines. A distance of sixty feet is common between ordinary cereal lines in the close pollinated plants and greater distances have to be maintained in regard to those which are open-pollinated.
It is fortunate that all these different types of plants have something which enables the onlooker to distinguish them. The matter of the shape of a plant is very important, and is perhaps the first thing noticed by the breeder or the man going into pure lines. ' All these different plants have different shapes. Even different varieties of wheat have different shapes. Some varieties are bearded; some are not. So that these different distinguishing characteristics are observed by these members of the Canadian Seed Growers' Association, in their special work. There is no great harm in having a plant with a different shape, except that it indicates cross-breeding. There is no great harm in a plant having a glume of a certain shape, any more than there is any great harm in a Holstein cow not having a white splash at the end of its tail. The white tip on its tail is simply an indication of pure breeding, and if an animal does not have that white tip you cannot register it. That is an indication of the breed, and the same thing occurs within limits in plant life.
As I say, these men are trained to detect these different changes. Such variations or off-types are severely dealt with in the examination of the plots by members of the seed branch. That is one thing I have not mentioned. The registration of plants is obtained in exactly the same way that we have registration of animals. Just as we get a registered Clydesdale or a registered Shorthorn, in the same way we get registered varieties of wheat, oats, vegetable seeds and so on. Pure lines

are obtained in this way, and certificates are issued. The Canadian Seed Growers' Association has the issuing of all these certificates, but the _ examination of the plots is done in cooperation with the scientific agriculturists of the Department of Agriculture. These men go around to the fields and examine them, in company with the grower and a representative of the association, and report what they find in the field. If sufficient impurities are in a field the field is not registered, and it is thrown out. Just there it may be of interest to hon. members to learn that a grower is allowed one plant in one hundred thousand slightly off type. In other words, his plot must be 99-999 per cent pure, which is extraordinary purity, reminding me somewhat of the C.C.F. party. Such purity is difficult to attain, as I am sure hon. members will agree.
Another point I should like to make is that somewhere there must be a source of pure seed, in exactly the same way that there must be a source of pure-bred animals. Certain men undertake to breed Hereford cattle. They keep the line pure, and other breeders know where to go if they want a purebred cow or bull. In exactly the same way you must have sources of pure-bred seed, and that source is the membership of the Canadian Seed Growers' Association. It must be quite obvious to hon. members that unless someone did carry on this work, very soon our strains would be all mixed up. We would have wheat, and that would be about the only way you could describe it, because it would be so badly mixed that we would not know what kind it was.
I wish to speak about this organization for a short time because I realize that it plays an important part in connection with the crops which are grown from seed in this country. Of the total of $2,146,000,000 I mentioned previously, some $1,120,000,000 represents crops grown from seed; that is, grain, vegetables and plants which have their origin in seed. So that it is quite important that this seed be kept pure. As far as the association is concerned, none of the officers receive any remuneration. The office staff, the secretary and those who are occupied in doing this work are the only ones who receive pay. The organization operates on a grant it has received for a number of years from this government. There was a time when the grant got as high as $25,000 per annum, and it will be noticed that in the estimates for this year the same amount is again being asked.
During the war years, however, it sank down to as low as $18,900. The organization has discovered it is not able to give service to its members on the allowance made to it at

As I have already said, it is being increased in the estimates from $18,900 to $25,000 for 1946. I believe that provision is allowed by the respective provincial governments.
Half of the officers of the organization are appointed by the different provincial departments of agriculture, and those departments take care of incidental expenses. First of all, I should like to commend the hon. member who has just taken his seat upon his interesting speech. It was most constructive and well poised. 1 found it a real pleasure to listen to what he had to say.
This afternoon we listened to an interesting debate on the various aspects of agriculture. To complete the picture I should like to say a few words and make a few suggestions to the Minister of Agriculture respecting another branch of that industry, namely the growing of sugar beets. I believe the minister can be of some assistance to us in bringing to the attention of hon. members and the people generally throughout Canada the fact that the process of growing sugar beets is more than just an industry.
At the present time I believe the people generally view the sugar beet industry as just another industry, such as a shoe factory or any other type of manufacturing concern. There is much more to it than that. It is not just a means of employing labour. I believe efforts should be made in the Department of Agriculture to make the production of sugar beets an integral part of the general agricultural programme of the country.
It is my sincere belief that there could be a closer relationship between the agricultural representatives in the government and the field men. May I make it perfectly clear that I am not criticizing agricultural representatives, either provincial or federal, realizing fully that they work under strenuous conditions. There are too few of them, and their districts are much too large. It is impossible for them to devote all their time to all branches of the industry.
Still, from the federal point of view, I believe a somewhat greater effort could be put forth to try, if nothing more, to publicize more generally the benefits of the sugar beet industry to farming as a whole. In those areas in the United States I have visited where sugar beet factories are operating, those factories have been made part of the general agricultural programme of the whole district. Those districts depend greatly upon the sugar beet factories, not only for sugar but for the general development of agriculture.
I believe the department could do much to publicize the various ways the beet tops and molasses can be used in the raising of cattle and in the dairying industry generally. Then, it can be argued that the growing of sugar beets is an effective means of cleaning the land and getting rid of weeds because, as we know, where sugar beets are grown every weed must be pulled by hand. Consequently, even if only fifteen or twenty acres are cultivated in that crop, that much land is clean at the end of the year. If that process is repeated every year the point is soon reached where the whole district surrounding the factory is entirely free of weeds. It is also a

most effective crop for those who .practise rotating their crops-and I believe we all do that. Certainly that is true in Manitoba.
I speak primarily, of course, for the sugar beet factory in Manitoba, which is relatively new. We had some difficulties, because we had to begin during the war. Labour conditions were hard to contend with and as an additional problem there were practically two total crop failures.

The sugar beet growers of this country have never been given a chance to put their case before the people of the country. I know I speak for the sugar beet growers' association and I believe also for sugar beet growers generally when I say that these people are most desirous of being given an opportunity to lay their case before a committee of this house. If that were done the country would become more conscious of this industry ; I was going to say this promising industry. It is a new industry as far as Manitoba is concerned, but it has bpen in existence for some time in other provinces and, as far as I can see, it is a successful industry.
If that were done it would go a long way toward removing many of the wrong concepts that people have about sugar made from beets. country would be directed toward the industry. I realize that there are many committees sitting during this session, for long hours each days and many days in the week. For a few minutes I should like to deal with the administration of the Rrairie. Faijp Assjgtance Act as it is applied to Manitoba. The administration of this act has resulted in many grievances in our province. It has been the source of misunderstanding. I doubt if there are many people who really understand the P.F.A.A. It is almost impossible to apply its provisions to Manitoba and the result is that all kinds of injustices are created. I know these are not intentional but, while the act may work to some advantage in Saskatchewan, in the wide-open spaces where the township is much smaller than in Manitoba, it has been impossible to apply it along the Red river valley where there have been total crop failures in the last two years.
I am not referring to what is ordinarily known as the Red river valley, I am referring only to the river lots and the first line of * quarter-sections on both sides of the river. First of all, the act does not provide for river lots and it is next to impossible to apply it where there are river lots instead of sections. The departmental officials have tried to block off the river lots into something like townships, but when that is done in a country that is rolling and has a definite slant toward the river, the effectiveness of the act is destroyed and it becomes ineffective. I have discussed this matter at great length with dominion and provincial officials in an effort to find a solution. I have tried to find some way to change the act so that it could be made applicable to my province but I have come to the conclusion that that is impossible. As far as I can see, the best thing to do is to cut Manitoba out entirely from the workings of the P.F.A.A.
I have gone to the trouble of compiling some figures from the annual reports of the P.F.A.A. starting with 1939 in an effort to get a comprehensive picture. I have tabulated the money received by the farmers, the money paid out by the farmers, the money paid out by the dominion and the money collected by the dominion for Manitoba,

Saskatchewan and Alberta. With the permission of the committee I could probably table these because I do not wish to read them all. They give a complete picture of what has happened since the inception of the act.
In the case of Manitoba, in 1939 a total of $333,000 was collected and $875,000 was paid out. I am giving only round figures. In 1940 they collected $355,000 and paid out $615,000. So that for those two years we were not losing. But from 1941 to 1945 the picture is entirely different. In 1942 nobody drew anything out of the fund in the three provinces. In 1943 we contributed $779,000 and drew out $30,000; in 1944 we contributed $755,000 and we collected $159,000. In 1945 I do not know exactly what the figure will be, but it would look as if we would contribute in the neighbourhood of $500,000 and draw out about $23,000.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that I am not talking of P.F.R.A., but of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which was passed primarily, I understand, to assist the drought area in Saskatchewan and applies exclusively to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The farmers are contributing one per cent of their grain sales toward the fund. Out of that fund they draw the moneys they receive. If the fund is not big enough the difference can be made up, I understand, by the dominion borrowing from the consolidated revenue fund.
So far as the dominion is concerned, it paid out in 1939 $10,000,000 and collected $2,000,000 ; in 1940 it paid out $7,000,000 and collected $2,000,000; in 1941 it paid out $15,000,000 and collected $1,500,000; in 1942 it paid out nothing and collected $2,700,000; in 1943 it paid out 86.500,000 and collected $4,700,000; in 1944 it paid out $6,000,000 and collected $5,385,000.
So that as far as the picture for the three prairie provinces as a whole is concerned I would take it that the act has been beneficial to Saskatchewan and Alberta, but so far as Manitoba is concerned we have contributed to the fund, in 1941, $303,000; in 1942,1482,000; in 1943, $766,000; in 1944 $600,000 and it looks very much as if we would contribute in 1945 between $400,000 and $500,000. Therefore it will be readily understood why I contend that this is not a good measure so far as Manitoba is concerned. There is a good reason for that. As I said at the beginning conditions in Manitoba are quite different from those in Saskatchewan and the township unit is far too big in relation to the average farm in Manitoba.
The picture presented by these figures looks brighter for Manitoba than it actually is
because up until 1942 the P.F.A.A., under its provisions, was paying out on the basis of 8 to 12 bushels to the acre when wheat was below eighty cents. If wheat goes over eighty cents the act provides only for payment on 0 to 4 bushels, $2.00, and from 4 to 8 bushels, $1.50.
If that were done, under conditons to-day we would not draw as much as we drew in 1939 and 1940. I respectfully submit to the minister that Manitoba be exempted from the P.F.A.A. because we have given up all hope of ever getting any benefit from it.
I will go one step farther and make a suggestion to the minister, if I may. Keep on collecting the one per cent on grain sales, if not the dominion, then by agreement with the province, to establish some form of crop insurance. I do not think that is the right term because it would not exactly be crop insurance, but I will use that term for lack of a better. If you kept on collecting the one per cent and put it into a fund, it could be made into a real crop insurance fund.
I have here a "Report on Crops, Live Stock, etc. produced in Manitoba in 1945." It was issued by the department of agriculture and immigration of Manitoba. It does not claim to furnish definitely reliable information but it is approximately correct. It gives a very fair picture of the crop and live stock production of the province. It also gives the hail damage done in Manitoba. I have taken the years from 1939 to 1945 and fitted them into this pattern to see how it would work out. I am not going to quote all the figures, but let us take the acreage that was totally lost by hail damage and the acreage partly lost from that cause in those years. I arbitrarily take the figure of $2 an acre for total loss and $1 an acre for partial loss by hail. This would have cost the province, in round figures, $106,500 in 1939; in 1940, $86,000; in 1941, $65,000; in 1942, $128,500; in 1943, $211,000. I do not like the term "insurance"-
Assistance.

I thank the minister. We could under my suggestion have given the farmers who were hailed out some assistance.

years-to more than one-fourth to one-third of the total amount which would be paid out. In other words, it was maintained that it was impossible-and at that time we thought the same idea might apply to Manitoba-to apply a purely insurance principle to payments required in connection with drought in areas so large as those affected in Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The question of insurance for crops had been under discussion in the west for many years, and many attempts were made to work out plans which could be based on the insurance principle; in other words, under which you could create a fund based on the payment of fees which at all times would meet the demands that were made upon the fund. But any figuring which was ever done with regard to the matter suggested the impossibility of ever being able to collect sufficient from farmers by way of fees to build up a fund large enough to take care of the losses that farmers incur in a year of serious drought.
I think it will be realized that to insure a man against the loss of his crop would be impossible in a year like 1937, for example, when a province which has a long-time average crop of sixteen to seventeen bushels an acre had an average crop of a little over two bushels to the acre. One can see what an enormous amount of money would be required in a fund to take care of a situation of that kind. So that after considerable discussion it was determined that the only way this could be looked after was for someone who had no opportunity ever to draw from the fund to be prepared to pay into the fund.
In view of the importance of wheat particularly and of grains generally to the economic position of the dominion, it was thought advisable, in order to avoid paying out great sums in relief, as was done in the years just preceding that over considerable periods, to have the dominion treasury made responsible for paying in from $3 to $4 for every dollar that would be paid by the farmers themselves. We have had an experience with that measure and are satisfied that a province like Saskatchewan cannot create a fund sufficiently large to make it possible for the province to take care of any losses related to drought.
I think the same is true of Alberta, but I believe it has been proved by the figures just quoted to the committee that there is a possibility that Manitoba could run its own insurance scheme. I rise to speak on the agricultural economy of Canada as it affects the individuals producing the foodstuffs of Canada as a whole. The production of foodstuffs is the world's number one industry to-day and it has always been the country's first industry. It has never been treated fairly by any government at Ottawa but rather has been held in contempt. All Canada has suffered from this treatment and will continue to suffer until agriculture receives the recognition it deserves. I am going to do some straight talking about the treatment the primary producer has received under this private enterprise system from both Liberal and Tory governments.
Full realization by the government of basic fundamentals is long overdue, and I think it is timely that a common dirt farmer should rise to speak in this house. I think I can qualify as one of those who come within that category, for the first twenty years of my life were spent on a farm in Ontario and the last thirty-four years in southwestern Saskatchewan in a part of the drought area.
Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that there are things that you can do in southwestern Saskatchewan and things that you cannot do. If some planning had been done by the government of that day, if settlers had been informed of the soil and weather conditions, and if there had been allotted economic units instead of wholesale half-sections on any kind of land there would have been very little relief needed or destitution in the southwest.

While I am on this question of plans, I should like to say this. I am sorry the government of to-day has not seen fit to use the results of the recent soil survey. Had that been done, there would have been a large increase in the acreage of wheat sowed this spring. Maps could have been got out and posted in Manitoba and the northern part of Saskatchewan and Alberta showing the black soil areas where summer-fallowing is done rather to keep down weeds than to conserve moisture. Thousands of acres of additional land could have been seeded this spring in those areas.
The southwestern part of Saskatchewan where I live, and most of the Palliser triangle where the brown soil runs from four to ten inches deep, is strictly a fifty per cent summer-fallow area; and it is simply tragic to practise anything else. I was glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture make a statement in the house the other day in connection with this matter. In this area, however, on the basis of half the land summer-fallowed each year-that is ten crops in twenty years- summer-fallowed by the right method, at the right time, early in May, average crops can be obtained. It is just as necessary to know thy land as it is to know thyself; and adaptability to the district is necessary.

This was after three short crop years in the west and particularly in the southwest. Our national revenue went down to $2,812,902,000 as compared with over $9,000,000,000 in 1944. At that time we had Tory governments in both Ottawa and Regina. The Winnipeg grain exchange was wide open. Free enterprise was going full blast. There were no ceiling prices, and no floor prices either. We had free intercourse with all the world and Bennett was going to blast his way into any market which was not open to us. There was only one country he would not deal with, and that was Russia; no truck or trade with Russia. Mr. Bennett would not even trade meat at 1} cents for oil.
That was the kind of thing we had in Canada in the midst of great potential wealth, the great natural heritage God gave his people in Canada. We had deprivation, hunger and want, with our children wandering over the land as bums and tramps, taking shelter in the lee of an elevator filled to the roof with wheat at from twenty to thirty cents; taking shelter in the lee of a warehouse filled with goods, boots, clothing and everything else; waiting for a freight train to come along after having been ordered out of town. Homes were broken up, and there were thousands in the soup kitchens. We had deportations and orders to leave Canada and go back to the old country. There was no place in Canada for immigrants. The other day our friends the Progressive Conservatives put up a vigorous verbal contest to retain Dominion day. I wonder if they were very proud of Dominion day in Regina in 1935.
Why shouldn't they be?
Perhaps the hon. member will change his mind in a moment. They were bidding for power that year, and if they had anything better to show it seems natural to me that they would have shown it.
Oh, oh.

This may be rather amusing, but from now on I do not think it will be as funny for my hon. friends I am going to place on record what was done by the champions of private enterprise; what was done for the unemployed at that time. I happened to be in Regina on July 1, 1935, when 3,300 young men were on what they called a trek to Ottawa bearing a humble petition asking for work and wages. They got only as far as Regina, and what happened?
They should have had something to eat.

The hon. member is right; they should. A meeting was called, and this is not very funny; there is a good deal of tragedy in it. Some person or persons called a meeting for eight o'clock on July 1 at Broad street park on Tenth avenue. Bills were posted up all over town saying, "Come to the meeting and help the boys on their way to Ottawa." At eight o'clock there was a big crowd there, including old men, women and people of all classes. I do not think there were over 400 boys there that night. There was a big ball game or football match where a good many Of the people were attending at the fair grounds where they were staying.
The chairman of the meeting had just introduced the speaker and immediately following that there was a commotion. People were diving here and there, and I wondered what it was all about. However, I saw what the trouble was, because a tear gas bomb had been pitched right in among the crowd of civilians who were there to attend the meeting. I looked around and I could see men in battle-dress, including tin hats and what looked like soft-ball bats in their hands. These men were rushing from furniture vans and other conveyances pulled up on the outside of the crowd, and they charged the crowd, an absolutely unprovoked assault. A policeman was killed, and a lot of other people were hurt and probably crippled for life. The street-cars were stopped; store windows were smashed. They battled all the way up Eleventh avenue to the post office.
There was nothing very funny about that, I can tell you. Just ask yourselves this:	If
all the 3,300 boys had been at that meeting, what would have happened? If my imagination serves me correctly, it would have been one of the blackest days in Canadian history. It would have been a black day if those boys had handled themselves the same as the 300 or 400 who were there.
I should be remiss in my duty if I did not say that it would be nothing short of a tragedy if anything like that were to happen again in this Canada of ours, because next time they will not be shirt-sleeved boys with little packs on their backs. They will be boys who have learned to fight. I say it was not the right thing to do. Shortly after that we had a Liberal government in power, both in Ottawa and Regina.

Later, farmers, 400 strong, bearing a petition on which there were 185,000 names, asked for increases in the price of wheat to meet the rising cost of production brought about by increases in the prices of things they had to buy. This is not a matter which can be traced only to a Liberal or Tory government at Ottawa. It is the result of the system, the private enterprise system. And Canadians are hogs for punishment if we put up with any more of it.
I will ask any hon. members where we would be to-night if the war had not come along and snapped us out of the private enterprise slump. Further, when this artificial war industry is over, when it is all cleaned up, can any member of the government show me where there will be any improvement? Can he show me any difference in the national economy to-day from what it was then, any difference that would justify our expecting anything better now than we had then?
More taxes.

Yes, one statement was made which we must not forget: We have about $20 billion more on which to pay interest than we had in prewar days.
Let us take another step in the economic history of this country. After agriculture had taken the terrific beating it did take, through low and ruinous prices which would not meet the cost of production, when it faced unpaid interest, worn-out machinery which needed replacements, buildings needing repairs, back taxes, accumulated mortgage indebtedness-when we faced all these things, we got this kind of treatment.
For example, in October, 1944, while the Canadian wheat board price of wheat was $1.43, the United States price was $1.83, indicating a net loss to the Canadian farmer of forty cents a bushel. Then, again, in October, 1945, with the Canadian wheat board price at $1.55, the United States price was $1.94, or a net loss to the Canadian farmer of thirty-nine cents. We will call it forty cents because since that time the price was around $2 in the United States. Our total exports for 1943-44 and 1944A5 were, roughly, 343,000,000 bushels in each year. When compared with what the United States farmer received, the Canadian farmer lost forty cents a bushel on each one of those bushels, or a total of $137,200,000. If Saskatchewan provided 52-2 per cent of that wheat, the loss to the Saskatchewan farmer was $71,344,000. Canada as a whole was able to show great generosity to the people of Europe at the expense of the western farmer. To use Mr. Churchill's formula, never have so few who were so poor given so much to so many.
The Saskatchewan farmer also played Santa Claus to the people of Canada. Canada uses about 50,000,000 bushels of wheat a year to feed her own people. Wheat was sold to the Canadian miller for $1.25 a bushel, f.o.b. Fort William. Then the miller obtained a subsidy or drawback from the government of 47% cents a bushel. This meant that the price to the Canadian people was 77% cents a bushel. Even members of parliament were able to eat cheap bread by being granted charity of sixty cents per bushel by the Canadian wheat grower and 47% cents by the government; but central Canada got cheap bread, so we can see that the wheat growers lost 50 millions at sixty cents, or $30,000,000. And, again, Saskatchewan farmers paid 52-2 per cent of this, or $15,600,000.

In addition, agriculture suffered an imposition of three cents a gallon on the fuel used in tractors, and this at a time when the industry was bankrupt. To add insult to injury, Saskatchewan has had to pay an additional two cents as well as a 12% per cent increase in the price of farm machinery. Little or no attention was paid when four hundred farmers brought a petition bearing 185,000 names to the government. The price of wheat was not fixed at $1.25 until it had gone above that figure on the open market. Yet we find that the oil companies and the machinery companies which enjoyed good profits in those years were able to sit behind closed doors with the government and receive sympathetic consideration.
Agriculture knew nothing about these increases until they were announced on the floor of this house by the Minister of Finance. Who is governing Canada? The people's representatives in parliament have no say in the laws that govern the economic well-being of the people of Canada. A farce has been made of our economic rights and we live under an economic dictatorship if there ever was one. Let us compare the treatment given to the agricultural industry with the government's treatment of the oil and implement industries.
In 1937 the net profit of Imperial Oil was $26,450,157; in 1938 it was $25,959,530. Those were the years in which we had two of the most disastrous crop failures Saskatchewan ever had. Did the Minister of Finance plead before parliament as he pleaded the case for the oil companies and the machinery companies? No, he did not, but I will tell you what he did. He arranged with the banks for the farmer to sign a blank note for his 1938 seed, which later proved to be $1.42 a bushel. The same wheat which had been delivered by the farmer and which had been sold for as low as sixty cents a bushel was still in the elevators; it was government owned wheat.
The government would not deal directly with the rural municipalities. Private enterprise had to get its toll. First the farmer had to sign a blank note. This was endorsed by the rural municipality, then by the provincial government and then by the federal government. The banks were then prevailed upon to accept the note. They had the security of the man on the farm and everything else in Canada.
Most of the wheat was in the pool elevators.

I am glad the cooperatives had something to do with it. Just what happened? The trade got the money and delivered government-owned wheat to the farmer for $1.42. On May 16, 1938, before the seed went into the ground, the average price for wheat went down to eighty cents a bushel at Eastend. I have documentary evidence of that from the dominion bureau of statistics, agricultural branch.
Right here let me say that when the Minister of Finance was pleading the case of the machinery companies in this house the other day he made a most ridiculous comparison. He said that wheat had increased 87 per cent, whereas the cost of machinery had increased only three per cent. The Minister of Finance knows very well that prices of machinery do not go up and down like prices of wheat. Those prices are stabilized; it is monopoly control, a law unto itself. Farm machinery prices have always been high or higher, whereas in 1940 the price of wheat was as low as forty cents a bushel. The minister could have improved his argument 100 per cent if he had gone back to 1932 when wheat was nineteen cents a bushel.

Good Liberal policy.

As I look around the house I see more than one member here who was born in Bruce county which I have the honour of representing, and I know that anything I say which will be to the benefit of Bruce county in the future they will support even if their party affiliations will not allow them to say so publicly. I should like to say to the hon. member for Maple Creek, who has just taken his seat, that he and I have some things in common, but a lot of things we have not in common. In his speech he back-tracked over a long number of years. That is the way of a pessimist. I like to be optimistic. But maybe the party to which the hon. gentleman belongs likes to capitalize on that kind of propaganda. Being a Progressive Conservative, I do not want to do that. I want to look ahead and not look back too far.
Bruce being a rural county, I feel proud to represent it, but the county has also some very good industries which are known internationally as well as nationally. I will mention a 'few of them. Keystone brushes are manufactured in Bruce county, and are known the world over. Furniture is manufactured in Bruce county at the Malcolm Furniture factory, and I believe some hon. members have enjoyed sitting on the company's products in this chamber; their furniture goes all over the world. We have in Bruce county knitting mills and dry spinning companies which are known internationally. All in all, I believe I am justified in a feeling of pride in being able to represent these fine agricultural districts of Bruce and Kincardine counties.
At the same time I must point out that circumstances in my riding are such that we are not happy. Centralization is working to our disadvantage. I mean that the farm population is gradually disappearing from our farming areas. The township I come from is a good township, and as I said before, Bruce

Supply-Agriculture
county is a good county. But within a mile and a quarter of the location of our farm, whereas in times I can remember there were thirteen families living in that area, at the present time we have only five. No doubt there are various reasons for that condition, but the principal reason is the lack of foresight which has been only too evident on the part of not only the present government but all governments which have administered Canada for a great number of years. I am not suggesting that any government has wilfully brought this about; yet it has happened. There is an idea in some quarters that mechanization in the line of farm work has had something to do with the depletion of our farm population. But is this so? Because of this machinery we do not have to work so hard; living conditions have improved, and it would follow that people would be happier to stay on the farms. But that has not been the case: we have lost a great part of our farm population. It cannot be said that mechanization is the cause of people leaving the farms. It will be found that the economic situation has more to do with conditions obtaining in that mile and a quarter in Kincardine township, in Bruce county, than anything else. We see there buildings which have been blown down by the wind; we see vacant houses and outbuildings where the roofs are going and which in a short time will be in an uninhabitable conditions. We have farms in need of reconditioning and farm buildings in need of repair. We have farms which need electrification. We have farms with no running water. I am not trying to paint an unduly dismal picture, but I am describing what is an actual condition in Kincardine township, and which I fear is typical of the average Canadian townships.
Working conditions on our farms are not satisfactory. On this point I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Maple Creek. He referred to the long hours which farm people have to work; I want to make a similar reference. Many of our farm population to-day are working too long for physical health and, in addition they are employing their children to help out. One reads in the newspapers of the exploitation of child labour in industry, but too little attention is paid to the exploitation of child labour on the farms; yet I venture to say that it is only too common, not as a matter of choice but from sheer necessity. The farmer's wife has never yet been able to get remuneration for the long hours and the heavy work which she has put in, in helping her husband on the farm. We have, therefore, this situation at the present time: the boys coming back from overseas who, under proper conditions, would be potential farmers are not going to farm. I know boys from our own district who would make good farmers, but the life is not attractive to them. Young people at the present time, owing to the unsatisfactory conditions they have to endure while being brought up on the farms, get away as soon as they can and try to find some place where they will enjoy better living conditions.
I do not want to take up the few minutes I intend to occupy without offering some suggestions to improve the state of affairs to which I have referred. If I may be pardoned for injecting a personal note I should like to say that Bruce county is a Scotch county.
That is all to its credit.

The hon. gentleman opposite has relatives in our county. I believe it has been in the habit of voting the Liberal ticket, but at the last election I was elected as a farmer Bracken candidate. Scotsmen are at times hard to convince, but on this occasion they saw the light, and I may add that I am not sorry for having been returned under these circumstances. The Progressive Conservative party has an agricultural programme which, in my opinion, when it is brought into effect after the next election, will gradually relieve the conditions which I have truthfully pointed out and which are in effect in our township at the present time; and these benefits will be shared not only by the farmers of Kincardine and Bruce counties but by all the people of Canada. I think hon. members will agree, because I am safe in saying that 99 per cent of them believe that the welfare of the farmer is the most important concern of dominion legislation. I do not need to repeat Mark Twain's saying, so think it over.
We hear a good deal about our great tourist industry and how many million dollars it is going to bring us. The best thing to do would be to put the men back on these farms to make a living for themselves and to get them away from conditions in the large cities which, while I will not describe them as unclean, are anything but joyful. Let them get back on the farms and make a little living for themselves, and that will be better for Canada than all the tourists coming in from neighbouring countries. So that I say to the government in power at the present time and to any government that we may have in the future-and I think I could accurately predict what government it would be-that we should keep in mind the fact that decentralization is of more importance to Canada at present than anything else that is on the agenda of the government to-day.
