I will be brief, and for once I am not critical because my first effort has been successful. Hon. members will see who has come to sit beside me. If I speak a little longer I shall probably have the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case) over to my left.
I did not say anything.

We have covered a lot of territory to-day and I want you to understand, Mr. Chairman, that anything I say to-night is fundamental, elemental and spoken in a kindly way. Let us be fair about this. We have heard a good deal to-day about sheep and we heard about the bargain basement. In a kindly way I want to speak too about sheep. When I was a boy going to school one of the chores I had to do was to look after sheep, and if any hon. members listening to me now have ever had to look after sheep they will know what a cantankerous animal a sheep can be. I remember one time when one of these sheep annoyed me and I hauled off and kicked as hard as I could, but instead of hitting the sheep I hit a cement pillar in the barn, and that nearly broke my foot. Ever since then I have made it my life's ambition to be kind to dumb animals. I hope no one will object to this remark.
As I have said, I am not here in a critical mood, but I wish to tell the Minister of Agriculture that his policy is all wrong. Outside of that, however, I think it is all right. The thing I am particularly interested in to-night is this-and I must say that I could not follow my hon. friend the member for Maple Creek because when I get up to $172 million that is as high as I can go. That does not mean anything to him. He can talk about $5 billion without any concern, but $5 billion

means quite a bit in the Fraser Valley. He said we are paying interest on $20 billion, but actually, it seems, it is only $15 billion. But $5 billion is neither here nor there to my hon. friend.
The reason I disagree with the Minister of Agriculture is the fact that he is not running agriculture. The wartime prices and trade board has too much to say, and the sooner agriculture is put back under the Department of Agriculture the happier we shall be in Fraser Valley. However, I am not going to be as dismal as some hon. members from Saskatchewan appear to be. My riding is one of the finest in Canada. There are many improvements that can be made, but most of the roofs are still on the houses and barns and on the whole we are very happy. We ought to be, because we produce almost half the berries that are grown in Canada, and they are the finest berries in Canada. I do not need to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that there is no necessity for us to camouflage our peaches in British Columbia in any way. We produce also seventy-five per cent of the hops produced in the dominion and as we do not know what to do with them we ship them out of the country. Altogether we are proud of that riding.
I thoroughly enjoyed the speech delivered by the hon. member for North Battleford. It was constructive and I was particularly interested in it in view of the fact that in my riding we have an immense production of bulbs. In fact, we pioneered the business in this country. We ship to eastern Canada bulbs not merely by the ton but by the carload. I heard one hon. member this afternoon, when we got away from the bargain basement and sheep, describe the tulips in front of the building here, and he accused the Minister of Agriculture, as I understood him, of being the gardener. Maybe that is the reason you have such teeny-weeny bulbs here. We have immense bulbs in my riding, and we ship them, as I say, by the carload. I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to devote a little more money and attention to assist us in finding ways and means of combatting diseases, because even in British Columbia we have had disease in our bulbs. His experts should pay a little more attention to this matter.
I am also interested in the question of milk. You know, Mr. Chairman, these subsidies that are spoken of as subsidies to the farmers are actually subsidies to the consumer. They are not subsidies to the farmers and I believe my friends of the C.C.F. will agree with me on that. In other words, they are not agricultural subsidies but consumer sub-

Supply-Agriculture
sidies. I believe the leader of the opposition will agree with me-if he does it is a credit to him-that the subsidy on milk is not high enough. I will not say what the arbitrary figure should be, but the Minister of Agriculture should exert a little more pressure on the treasury board in order that the subsidies be set on farm produce prior to any increases being put, as in the case of machinery, on what we have to buy in order to produce anything on the farm. They started at the wrong end.
We are a little worried in British Columbia about the consistency of some of our hon. friends immediately opposite me. Regina is a small town somewhere in Saskatchewan;
I believe they had a convention once, and we have been spending days here discussing a bill of rights. I am sorry that has come from Saskatchewan too, but they have been suggesting a bill of rights, or a new constitution or charter or something. They seem to have a habit in Saskatchewan of doing that sort of thing. At any rate, plank No. 6 in the manifesto of their convention had reference to cooperative institutions. I am not going to read it all because I do not want to give them the benefit of such free advertising, but they speak of encouragement by public authority of both producer and consumer cooperative institutions.
Coming from British Columbia, I cannot understand that, although in that province the C.C.F. and their bad boy Harold Wmch want to socialize milk. Can you imagine that? And how do they propose to do this? I would like the hon. member for Regina City to answer that. The board would have power to expropriate all existing plants and equipment, including distribution facilities for crude milk, and operate them. We in the Fraser valley, which includes part of the riding of the hon. member for New Westminster, produce 90 per cent of the milk of the province of British Columbia, and we have the largest dairy cooperative in Canada distributing that milk. But they are going to take us over and socialize us.
Isn't that socialized in that set-up? What are you talking about?

I was just hoping the hon. member would say that, because it will get me a thousand C.C.F. votes at the next election. We have this cooperative; they have their charter, and now the C.C.F. are going to do away with cooperatives by socializing the production of milk. There in British Columbia we have forty-eight members
And no Liberals.
We have a Liberal premier, and we had for a long time-

If the hon. member will permit a question, does he know that in the time the C.C.F. government has been in power in Saskatchewan cooperatives have increased at a greater rate than ever before, and with the blessing of the C.C.F. government?
Oh, you are dreaming; it isn't true.

I should like to answer that question. I understand they set up a ministry to encourage cooperatives, and I bless them for that. It is too bad they were not in power before, when horses were selling for $27; they would have canned them. Here is your manifesto. However, I am not talking about Saskatchewan; my dairy farm in my riding is in British Columbia. The C.C.F. party in that province, at their convention on April 29, declared their policy to be the socialization of milk.
Hear, hear.
There is one blessing about it. They will never be in power in British Columbia.
Where are the Liberals in British Columbia now? I licked the last one up in Prince Rupert last fall.
What about Mr. Hart; is he Conservative or Liberal?
If Mr. Hart ever desires to retire-well, I am modest, and I shall not say what I was going to say.
He came from the Conservative party.

Oh, no. My hon. friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs sat in a Liberal cabinet with him about twenty years ago, I think.
However, I have brought out my point, and now I shall go on with my story about milk. There are some forty-eight members in the province of British Columbia, only two of whom represent producing areas. You people follow that through, as I hope the producers will follow it through and as I know the producers in the Fraser valley are following it through. I am quoting the very C.C.F. people there, who say, "If they put that in, we are wiped off the map." As I say, of the forty-eight members only two represent producers and forty-six represent the consuming public. No wonder Harold Winch would put that in. How do you suppose they would set the price? They would set it regardless of the

welfare of the producers. We would be back in the days of six-cent eggs and twenty-eight cents for butterfat if the price were set by the forty-six members to the detriment of the two members. You cannot laugh that one off, though I do not know where you get this figure of six-cent eggs.
However, I believe in giving the C.C.F. a fair deal in this house, and I refer now to one of the largest and best weekly papers in Canada. I would say it is the best; only I have five in my riding. Here is what the C.C.F. said at the provincial convention, according to this newspaper: "Other delegates charged cooperatives do not consider the consumer." This is the C.C.F.; the cooperatives do not consider the consumer! You must have a different brand of cooperatives in Saskatchewan from what we have in British Columbia.
However, I should like to mention something in which I fully agree with faon. gentlemen opposite. In this debate today I think we have covered every subject except agriculture, though we have missed out on the banks. We used to have a member from Vancouver-Burrard who went over to the holy of holies, and who represented us as far as the banks were concerned. We have covered all these other subjects to-day, but I want to point out to the Minister of Agriculture that I entirely agree, as I believe every other hon. member will, that unless the government stabilize agricultural prices; unless they guarantee the farmer a fair price in relation to the prices of everything he has to buy, the veterans coming back from this war are not going to settle on our farms. That is true in my province, and I think it is true in every other province. Personally I belive the system of subsidies is all wrong. I think the solution of the problem of the farmer is to pay him a fair parity price in comparison with the cost of the things he has to buy in every branch of his production.
.That is the C.C.F. programme you are quoting now.

I was in politics long before the C.C.F. were heard of, and perhaps they copied part of my programme. However, I am glad my hon. friends agree with me; some day they might even invite me to lead their party out of the wilderness. I want to say to the minister seriously that I was surprised to find there have been only forty-eight applications for farms in my own riding under the Veterans Land Act'. I fully expected there would be manY'lrfo'rb, but speaking from memory I believe only some seventeen have qualified and been granted farms. When you have a riding

which is almost entirely agricultural; when you have from that riding, I say without fear of contradiction, an enlistment of farmers' sons as great as that in any riding in Canada-I do not say "greater" but as great-it is surprising to me that prior to April 15 there should be only forty-eight applications for farms under the act. The remedy is for this government or whatever government is in power-and we are in power at present, so it is our responsibility-to guarantee these men not subsidies but prices which will afford a decent standard of living and which will permit them to carry out their obligations and manage the debt they will be called upon to undertake if they are to settle upon farms. We should not repeat what happened after the last war, when veterans bought $200 cows and had to pay for them with butter-fat at twenty-eight cents a pound. I think it is the duty of this government to see that our returning young men are given this guarantee. This government has gone to this extent, and I am proud to say so. It is the first government to put floor prices under farm products. That is a wonderful step in the right direction, but I think the government should now carry it further and guarantee the farmer prices for his products before it permits any increases of any kind on the things the farmer requires to buy.
I just wish to close by saying that I have nothing to be ashamed of or to apologize for in my riding, like hon. gentlemen opposite seem to have in connection with their ridings. We are proud of the condition of our riding, but we want to make it better. We have every class of citizen there, and we want every class of citizen except one. We shall be glad to give that class to Skeena, if they want them, or to the rest of Canada, but that is the only class we do not want.
A true Liberal.
Well, we have never promised them the vote in order to get their financial or other support.
Why are not more soldiers anxious to get back to Fraser valley on the farms?

I am sorry the hon. member for Mackenzie did not get the point before. I do not think a soldier can afford to pay what our land costs unless he has some better guarantee in relation to what he is going to receive for his products, and that is what I am putting to the government. I do not mean a guarantee for this month or six months from now; I mean a guarantee for five or six years from now. Another reason the soldiers are not anxious to get back on the land is that they cannot afford to buy the

land for a normal dairy farm, or anything other than a small holding in the Fraser valley, with the present ceiling under the Veterans Land Act. If my hon. friend had led the life some of these young boys have led I believe he would understand this also. I do not think you will find many of these young men, as I am sure the hon. member for Skeena will agree, ready to go away up north, where the pioneers went in the years gone by. I am not knocking that country, but I do not think you will get young men to go up there until such time as transportation, electricity and all the other modern facilities are put through. That is one reason they are not going back to the land. I want to tell the hon. member for Mackenzie that some 75,000 veterans in other parts of Canada have either taken their discharge or want to take their discharge in our fair province. And most of them want to come to the Fraser valley.
And they are unemployed, remember that.

I wish to make a few remarks at this time. I was pleased to hear the minister tell the committee how the packers made a $10 change in the price of a steer across Canada. I have been arguing that right along, namely that we have no price set on the live animal. He has been doing that right along. The minister never said a more truthful word than he did the other evening.
The question with which we are faced these days is this: Is the packer getting enough? I think he is getting more than enough. I have thought for a long time that he is getting more than enough.
Let us take a 1,000-pound steer-
I should like about five pounds of it.
Oh, I have treated you to a good steak before, so keep quiet.
Right.
No.
Oh, yes, they have failed to do that.
They are on the market all the time.

Yes, but they are not on their job, because animals have been selling for eleven cents when they should be twelve cents. The minister has accused me of spending more time around the stockyards than around my farm. Surely he will give me credit for knowing something about the stockyards, if what he has said is true.
That is our big trouble to-day; we have a ceiling on beef. When it comes into the hands of the packer it is protected by the wartime prices and trade board. That is unfair. Let us take that nonsense about lambs last year, when your board agreed to buy up all the surplus lambs at a quarter-cent less than the market. What good did it do to the market?
Supply-Agriculture

It did not amount to anything to the farmer, because the packer could buy them from the farmer at whatever price he liked. When a man sends 200 lambs to the market he does not take them back 200 miles because he gets a cent less. He will let them go at the price, and also say a lot of hard things about the Minister of Agriculture.
I am sure the minister understands the situation. I do not know whether he has tried to correct it. At different times I have tried to explain it. I have said it has been the cabinet which has brought about a condition under which the minister cannot meet what the farmer wants. It would seem that the cabinet dominates the Department of Agriculture; if not, the wartime prices and trade board would not have the power it has to-day.
I had some questions to ask the minister about cattle going to the United States. He has assured me that that market has been taken care of and that we shall be able to get it back when we have more cattle to dispose of. The United States market is our best market to-day; we have no better. But I believe we are going to have more cattle than the United States quota will handle, and we shall have to look for further markets.
I am suggesting to the minister that we do some research into the matter of sending live cattle to Great Britain. It would pay the farmers if that were done. Remember, I am maintaining that the United States market is our best market, combined with that here at home. But we shall have extra cattle, and if we can sell them to Great Britain, so much the better. We could land in Great Britain cattle which, in Canadian funds, and less the bonus of five shillings per hundredweight which they are paying at the present time-I am not adding that five shillings- would bring us about 814 per 112 pounds.
Some hon. members might say that there has to be a profit there. There does not need to be any profit. If you can land them there at a price, the farmer is prepared to take them at that price because the manure he gets from the feeding of the animal will pay him in three months for his labour and feeding costs. He will get his expenses and his feeding costs, because he feeds those steers for the sake of the fertilizer he can get.
I repeat that we should have some research done, and that the department should do it. On previous occasions the minister has given me literature dealing with this matter. The more I read about it, the more I see in it. When I was in the old country this year I was convinced that there is a good market over there for good steers. Perhaps we can ship them out through Hudson bay and thus reduce freight costs, which would be a great advantage.

I was going to say something about sugar beets but the hon. member for Provencher has pretty well covered the subject. I agree with what he said but he did not touch upon the labour situation. I hope the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Labour, who, I notice, is in his seat, have given that matter serious consideration. The production of beets requires more labour than anything, else we do on the farm. Huge commitments have been made in order to ensure the success of the sugar beet industry from one end to the other of the Red river valley in Manitoba, and I hope the two ministers will cooperate so that we can get the labour that is necessary.
Last year and the year before I asked the Minister of Agriculture about the payment of the wool bonus to Manitoba, but my pleas fell on deaf earsbecause the provincial government has not agreed to pay its share. It is contended that if the provincial government will pay two cents, the dominion government will match it. I am going to appeal to the minister not to make a stepchild out of Manitoba. If he is paying two cents to Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia he should pay two cents to Manitoba and shame the provincial government into paying the other two cents. You cannot produce wool cheaper in one province than in another, and the non-payment of this bonus is a detriment to the production of sheep and wool in Manitoba. You have no idea how it is talked about, and if this bonus was paid I am sure it would create a favourable impression toward the Liberal government, if that could be an argument. I have asked this of the minister before and I hope he will give it his consideration. When the dominion government makes this concession to other provinces it is only right that it should make it to Manitoba.
When the minister speaks I should like him to tell me whether the subsidies that will be paid from April 30 are to be paid from money voted in connection with the Agricultural Prices Support Act?
No.
When is that act to come into operation?
It has been declared in effect now.
There is no money being paid out of it whatever?
No.

In dealing with the milk situation, I can speak only of the Winnipeg area. On the orders of the day there has been some discussion about milk producers asking that the winter subsidy be carried through the summer. I think the minister replied that you

Supply-Agriculture
would have to even up the price, but I should like to correct that. The milk producers do not want that price evened up, what they want is the winter price carried through and a new price negotiated for next winter. Do not let us have any misunderstanding about that. As someone said a little while ago, the cost of labour has gone up. It may be said that while I am against the packer getting a rise in price, I am asking for an increase for the milk producer. The fact is that the milk producer is working under entirely different conditions to-day. The men who milked cows before they went to war will not milk them now that they have come back. They know that a factory worker works for only eight hours a day and they just do not want the fifteen or fourteen-hour day on the farm.
People in Canada to-day realize that milk is the cheapest food in the world. You cannot get anything as cheap that contains the same amount of nourishment or that gives such a balanced diet. At one time I used to fight in Winnipeg for a milk foundation, but I do not think we are going to need it because the people have been educated to use milk. They are beginning to know what a good thing milk is; they know that in order to be strong in body and mind, the person who drinks lots of milk is well on the way.
Let me show how the demand for milk has increased. In March, 1945, there was shipped into the Winnipeg area a total of
9,960,000	pounds of milk. In March, 1946, those shipments were up to 11,500,000 pounds. In March a year ago there were 910 producers in the Winnipeg area; to-day we have 1,290, an increase of 380. Those additional 380 milk shippers should produce far more milk because they have better cows in the Red river valley to-day than they had ten years ago or even five years ago; the cattle are heavier producers.
The fact is that the big dairy producers, the men who were milking fifty, sixty or seventy cows, found that they could not get help and had to sell out. The cows were purchased by smaller shippers, men who were willing to work and who were willing to have their families work. Surely in a modem world like this we do not need to exploit a man's family in order to produce milk for the nation, but that is what is taking place. You cannot get a hired man to milk cows and the result is that the large dairy farmer is going out of business.
I remember the time in the Winnipeg milk area when there was a straggle to get a quota. Nobody worries about quotas now because you get paid for every pound of milk you send in. The trouble is to get somebody to buy your cows and your milk quota and get rid of them. Reference has been made to
the rise in the price of machinery, but that is only a minor thing compared with the help situation. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister, and I want to impress upon him that an adequate price must be paid for milk next winter or we shall have milk rationing in Canada. I hate to think that there will ever be such a thing as milk rationing in Canada; but unless the producer of milk is subsidized or his business is made profitable enough to warrant his staying in business, that is what will happen. I told hon. members that when I was in Britain I saw that children under twelve years of age were getting half a pint of milk a day. We do not want that in this country. If the production of milk is put on a profitable basis it provides a good living. There are plenty of people who like to milk cows but they do not want to milk them for nothing. You just cannot afford to pay factory wages and give factory hours. I heard someone on the other side say that he had offered $100 a month and board but could not find anyone to take it.
These are things we are up against in the Red river valley at this time. I commend these remarks to the minister and I hope he will answer them when he speaks.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to speak in this debate to-night, but I felt someone should answer the hon. gentleman to my right who on numerous occasions has made slighting and insulting references to one of the most distinguished parliamentarians that this country has ever produced, Miss Agnes Macphail. Every once in a while someone to my right who has not the courage to rise in his place and say it, growls some slighting remark about Miss Macphail. It reminds me of the story told of a meeting at which Miss Macphail was heckled by a very little man. Finally he said, "Miss Macphail, don't you wish you were a man?" She replied, "Sure, don't you?"
One of the most shocking attitudes that I find in this house from time to time is this, that when there are people who have the courage and integrity to expose something of which we should all be ashamed, instead of our trying to get to the root of the matter and attack the evil, we attack the person who exposes the evil.
Recently we have been hearing a lot about British traditions. We have several kinds of British traditions, but the finest kind of British tradition that we have is the tradition of establishing new precedents of justice, the tradition of being able to recognize injustice and to make the necessary changes. That is the only British tradition that I am proud to
Su-p-ply-Agriculture

admit, and I must say that all my ancestors were Britishers, but I take no credit for that because I had nothing to do with it.
There are people in this house who seem to think western Canada is the poor relation, and the only time we hear from them is when they want something. I should like to quote some figures given by Doctor F. H. Auld, deputy minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan, when speaking of the dominion-provincial conference. He was the deputy minister under the last administration, a man whom we retained because he was valuable. He had this to say about the contribution that western Canada makes to the economy of Canada as a whole:
Western Canada was well to the fore in the production of foodstuffs, he said, and cited the fact that one-third of the creamery butter and one-half of the hogs produced in the dominion came from the prairie provinces. Other examples cited by Dr. Auld were that the west produced 55 per cent of all cattle, 60 per cent of the sheep, 50 per cent of the sugar beets and 40 per cent of the honey produced in Canada.
For that we from the west do not need to apologize.
I am not going to extend my remarks, but I promise to make a speech every time that anybody laughs about the Regina riots. If anybody thinks civil war is funny they have never witnessed it. We would not have the effrontery to laugh if the name of a man who died overseas were mentioned in this house. We would bow our heads in tribute to one who had died in defence of his country. The men who died because of the Regina riots were just as much casualties, only they were casualties of poverty, unemployment and injustice, and the people who spoke and worked in defence of those unfortunate unemployed boys deserve better than to be ridiculed and scorned by any member of this house.

Mr. Chairman, coming from the agricultural county of Northumberland I am pleased to have an opportunity of saying a few words about agriculture, which is our basic industry in this country.
The farmers of Canada did a big job in feeding this nation through the war years, and they are continuing to do a big job in production. But if that is to be continued it appears to me that it will be necessary to make farm prices attractive in order to assure a supply. We have had peiling prices on most of our farm products, but the farmers feel that those ceiling prices were put on before prices of other products in this country had reached their peak.
I was interested in hearing the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon speak of the export of our cows and heifers to the United States and of the cow population in this country. But I question very much the accuracy of

the figures he gave of our cow population. I do not just see how he arrives at his figures. Of course, we have a bureau of statistics which sends out circulars covering a cross-section of the country, but I would not say that the bureau's cow population figures are the actual figures. I am inclined to believe, judging from our dairy production and the butter shortage and other things, that our cow population is less than the figures given by the minister. We know that we have had a shortage of butter. This can be attributed largely to government policy. The farmers who were producing butterfat and all of us are ready to admit that it was necessary to ship cheese to Britain in view of our commitments during the war, but the war has been over now for some time and the thousands of farmers in this country who are producing cream to be manufactured into butter should not be put at the disadvantage under which they have laboured for the last two years. We are the greatest butter eaters in the world in Canada. We have our home market and we should see to it that the people of this country get sufficient butter. I am satisfied that if the prices of our dairy products were put on a fair basis we' should- get all the butter we require.
We have heard considerable in this house about the housing shortage. Let me say, coming from one of the rural parts of this country, that we have in the rural parts many, many homes that are empty. Possibly the housing shortage in the cities has been caused in part by people leaving the farm and going into the urban centres. They are not now returning to the farm; the farmers who did stay on the land and have modern machinery have, in many cases, purchased the farm beside them and consequently the house on that farm is empty. It seems to me that if we are to get our people back on the farm to engage in agriculture it will be necessary to make agricultural prices attractive enough to bring them back.
One hon. member to-night mentioned the tourist business and said that it did not make very much difference. I believe the tourist business is something that we should encourage. The county of Northumberland . from which I come is bounded on the south by lake Ontario and on the north by Rice lake and the Trent river, and we have many tourists coming there each year. That is true of many other parts of Ontario and, no doubt, of Quebec. These tourists buy a great deal of farm produce, and it certainly means something to agriculture. We should do everything in our power to encourage tourists to visit our country.

It is regrettable that more veterans are . not going back on the farms. From the county of Northumberland there are very few; I do not believe they average one to each of the nine townships in the county. There must be some reason why these young men are not returning to agriculture. I strongly suggest that in any policy laid down for agriculture adequate prices be considered.
I am satisfied that if fair prices were assured many of our veterans would go in for farming.
We have heard something about the deplorable state of conditions in western Canada where they work from sixteen to seventeen hours a day. I have been operating a farm for a good many years, and I have never found that one could get the best from men or horses from operating that long. I believe better results could be obtained with much shorter hours; and, with the modern machinery we have, I do not believe anything will be gained by painting to our younger men such a picture as that it is necessary to work for sixteen or seventeen hours a day to make a living.
I am pleased, Mr. Chairman, to have had an opportunity of contributing these few remarks to this debate.

In rising to speak to-night to the committee on the subject of agriculture, I had intended to begin my comments by saying something about the Canadian seed growers' association.
I wish to compliment the hon. member for North Battleford on the address which he gave and in which he dealt so fully with that subject. I have compiled a number of figures regarding the work of the association, but I am not going to detain the committee this evening with them.
The hon. member for North Battleford dealt with seeds which are grown and used within Canada. I wish to say a word or two about seeds which are exported, and with which he did not deal so fully. The figures I will quote were supplied by the agricultural supplies board and relate to the crop year ended June 30, 1945. They dealt with alfalfa, red clover, alsike, sweet clover, brome grass, crested wheat grass, timothy, Canada blue grass and creeping red fescue. The. total value of these exports amounted to $5,571,289. Along with that were exports of flaxseed to the value of $203,000, flaxseed for commercial use to the value of $3,656,000, potato seed to the value of $5,464,679, and seed grains not otherwise listed, $1,548,000. As I said before, this does not include the value of seed grain sold and used in Canada. So that.I think the small appropriation to the Canadian seed growers' association of some 63260-88
twenty-five or thirty thousand dollars is an extremely fine investment for the Department of Agriculture to make, and if all the investments of the government brought returns in the same proportion we would be getting somewhere.
I also wish to make a few remarks regarding the agricultural picture as I see it, representing as I do a constituency not entirely rural, but a constituency, as are many others in Canada, dependent upon the farmer for food. May I also emphasize that they are dependent on the farmer for prosperity. Too often in the past we have heard it said, "Give labour high wages and they will buy the farmers' produce." But if you give the farmer a decent price for his product he will buy the articles produced by labour'. In the past you have the thing all backwards.
They depend on one another.

Let me refer particularly to the agricultural policy in its relation to the wartime prices and trade board and, in particular, to Mr. Donald Gordon. Agriculture subsidies are an admission on the part of this government that prices were inadequate as of October 20, 1941, when price ceilings were fixed. A simple announcement at that time to the consumer public that if the world wanted to eat they would have to pay a fair price for the food they required, would have setled the matter right ijhen and done away with all agricultural subsidies. I think the government, as is its practice in many other matters, looked around to see what would be politically expedient and then framed its subsidy policy. The present government knows very well and its advertisements and proaganda have shown that it was attempting to channel off purchasing power in consumers' hands.
At the outbreak of war, and ever since, the government has taken the attitude of not taking the public into its confidence. It would sooner wait and see what political advantage could be gained. The very time it was instituting subsidies of all kinds to maintain these so-called price ceilings was a time when people were better able to buy food than ever before because practically everyone employable was working in industry.	.

It will be noticed that Canadian farmers in about the same period referred to by the Minister of Agriculture were able to reduce their indebtedness by only some $6 million. I therefore have grave doubts whether the farmer's condition is as rosy as the minister would like us to believe.
I spoke of Donald Gordon and agricultural subsidies. We hear a great deal of his alleged ability. We shall be better able to judge his ability twenty-five years hence. He should be compelled to reduce the debt of Canada by the amount of all the farm subsidies paid out unnecessarily to maintain a price ceiling that

was not maintained. The amount of these subsidies runs into many millions. In 1944 alone it was $104,552,761 on items given in a statement by the dominion bureau of statistics.
I also stated that the price ceiling was not maintained and I make that statement for two reasons. First of all, the quality of practically all farm products has been maintained and, in some lines, improved, while the quality of many things the farmers buy has depreciated considerably. I will mention only a few items: lumber, coal, supplementary farm feeds and clothing. Not only that, but according to the dominion bureau of statistics when dealing with the cost of living index taxes are not considered, and I believe that about 30 per cent of the income of the Canadian people goes in taxes, so that this becomes a considerable item.
Let me quote a few comparisons taken from advertisements of food in the London Free Press of the week of October 16, 1941, and from the same type of advertisements in the same paper from the beginning of this year, and in most cases for the same retail food store advertisements as in 1941. These are some of the prices quoted in the London Free Press of October 16, 1941: prime beef brisket, pot roast, nineteen cents; since January 1, 1946 it has been twenty-three cents; shoulder roast, prime rib roast, twenty-five cents in 1941 and to-day, thirty-nine cents; porterhouse steak, thirty-three cents in 1941 and now forty-three cents; sausages, twenty-seven cents in 1941 and to-day, thirty-five cents.
In these quotations, I would point out that while the ceiling has been pierced as far as these finished products are concerned, the price of farm products the farmer sold has gone up but little in comparison. Hams were selling at that time at twenty-seven cents; to-day they are forty-four cents; veal at that time was twenty-four cents and since January 1, 1946, thirty-five cents in retail stores. With these prices going up in that way, without any increase as far as the farmer is concerned, the farmer is placed in a serious position. I thought I would take this opportunity of bringing these facts to the attention of the minister.
